column9: A wood engraving of two of the Alert's people standing in a ring of stones on a raised beach, one of them lifting a stone. Moss's facing text is one of the earliest published readings of these features: he records not fixed habitation but the traces of a migrating people whose hunters travelled far with dog sledges, notes the broken walrus and seal bones lichen-grown beside them, argues that no mere hunters would need such a town of huts nor build on a new site at each visit while leaving the circles of stone beside them, and reports similar remains far westward through the Parry group. These are Thule and earlier Inuit tent rings; the stone circles and the bone are what archaeologists still record.

A wood engraving of three stone cairns on the low summit of Washington Irving Island, with two men of the Alert standing beside the tallest. The cairns are not the expedition's own; they stood there when the ships came, and the same island was where Greely's party in 1881 recovered Nares's records of 1875 and 1876 from a cairn.

column5: A Ravine in the Stratified Ice
column9: Two wood engravings on one page. The upper, unlettered, shows a driver flat on his face being dragged at the heels of his eight-dog team after the traces were loosed from the sledge; Moss's text says the dogs divided on either side of a lump of ice and so put an end to his Mazeppa-like career. The lower, captioned, shows a man standing in a ravine cut through the stratified ice near Floeberg Beach.

A small wood engraving, signed and dated by Moss on the plate, of a sledging camp with two tents and a dog team on the floes, the distant pack lifted into flat bars by mirage. The printed list dates it 7 April 1875; the sledge journey it belongs to was made in April 1876.

A wood engraving of the grave of Niels Christian Petersen, the Danish-Greenlandic interpreter and dog driver of HMS Alert, on the top of a small hill between the beach and the beacon on Cairn Hill at Floeberg Beach. Moss records that Petersen, already maimed by frost-bite, was the first of the expedition to die of scurvy, on 14 May 1876; the ground was frozen as hard as rock and it took three days' work with pick and gunpowder to dig a grave three feet deep, and the spot was chosen because a long heavy slab suitable for a tombstone lay there. The headboard carries a cross.

column5: The North Coast of Greenland, from Cape Britannia to the mouth of Robeson Channel and Cape Rawson
column9: A two-part panorama sketched by Moss from the main-top of HMS Alert at her winter quarters, running from Cape Britannia at the extreme left of the upper section to the mouth of Robeson Channel and Cape Rawson at the right of the lower. It is a coastal profile of the whole north Greenland shore that Beaumont's and later Lockwood's sledge parties walked, drawn from the masthead of a ship frozen in at 82 degrees 27 minutes north. Position is a point on the coast the panorama covers.

A wood engraving from a sketch Moss made near midnight on 2 August 1876, looking back along the Alert's track: the ship small under a black headland, threading a lane between the grounded bergs of the ice-foot and the closing floes. Two days later, walled in by bergs in Shift Rudder Bay, the ice forced her up on the ice-foot, heeled her over and damaged her rudder.
